title: Design QA before a site goes live
metaTitle: Design QA on the site you will ship
excerpt: Design QA means using the real pages on a phone: forms, empty states, titles, and type at the size you will ship. A Figma walkthrough does not catch what a customer will hit.
alt: A laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, beside a plant and a yellow mug, the shipped page rather than a picture of the page.
caption: A laptop, a plant, and a yellow mug. Design QA happens on the site you will ship. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should design QA cover before launch?
faqs.answer: Follow the buyer's path on the production URL, on a phone and on a desk. Submit forms with good and bad data, open empty and error states, and read the type at the size you will ship. Check titles, links, and the email the form sends.

faqs.question: Is a Figma review enough to sign off a site?
faqs.answer: No. A file can be approved and the site can still fail a customer. Layout shift, a missing error message, and a title left over from staging show up on the real URL. Check the fix on that URL again before you call it done.

faqs.question: Who should do the QA pass?
faqs.answer: The person who designed the page, a second person who did not, and the founder on the path they will tell people about. Write findings as defects with an owner. A new page idea that appears during QA is a swap or a later phase, not a silent addition.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results
How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Design QA is a pass over the real site, on a phone and on a desk, before you tell anyone it is live. Check the pages, the forms, the empty states, and the type at the sizes you will actually ship. A website design qa checklist that lives only inside Figma will pass a file and fail a customer.

Open the production URL. Click the path a buyer takes. If you only present the frames, you have not done QA. You have done a review of a picture of the site.

## The pages a stranger can reach

Start from the first screen and follow every primary link. Homepage, offer, proof, price or the shape of the price, and the way to start. Then the footer. Then a direct URL to a deep page, because many people will not arrive at the homepage.

On each page, read the heading and the button. They should match the offer you think you are launching. A redesign that kept an old sentence in the hero is a QA find, not a content nit. A new offer that still wears the old title in the browser tab is the same kind of find.

Check the title element against the visible heading. Google's guidance on title links says every page needs a descriptive title, and that a title which does not match the page is a common reason Google shows something else. Half-empty titles, last year's date, and the same boilerplate on every URL all show up in this pass. Fix them before you announce the launch.

Open the site on a phone on cellular, not only on the studio wifi. Look at the first screen without scrolling. Can you tell what this is and what to do? Nielsen Norman Group's finding is still the bar: people often leave in 10 to 20 seconds, and the value has to be clear in about 10. A hero that only works as a full-bleed desktop crop has failed QA even if the Figma frame was approved.

Hit the states you already scoped. Empty search. No results. Sold out. Form error. Form success. A long name in a card. A missing image. If a state was in scope and it was never designed, that is a gap in the work, not a reason to skip it. If it was out of scope, confirm the plain default is acceptable, in writing, before launch.

## Type, space, and the things that move

Read a paragraph on the phone. Then read it on a laptop. The size, the line length, and the contrast should hold in both places. A display face that looked sharp in a frame often becomes a headline you cannot read at arm's length. QA is allowed to send a headline back. That is the point of doing this before launch rather than after the campaign starts.

Check spacing where content is real. The draft in the design file was a polite length. The client's real sentence is longer. Buttons wrap. Cards collide. A navigation label overflows. Use the real words in QA, not the lorem from the first workshop. If the real words are not ready, the site is not ready, even if the layout is.

Watch the page load. Does the layout jump after the type arrives? Does a banner push the button? web.dev defines the Core Web Vitals as three measures of the experience, with thresholds aimed at the 75th percentile of visits. Largest contentful paint, the loading measure, should occur within 2.5 seconds. Interaction to next paint should be 200 milliseconds or less. Cumulative layout shift should be 0.1 or less. You can feel the third one without a lab: if the page moves under a thumb, it fails the spirit of the check. Confirm the numbers in the field tools you have, and treat a lab score as a clue, not as the whole truth. web.dev is explicit that lab measurement does not replace field measurement, because devices and networks differ.

Motion gets the same pass. Anything that moves should have a reason, and a reduced-motion path should leave the page usable. A Hanabi build uses Motion where it helps and keeps that path. QA includes turning reduced motion on and confirming the offer is still there. An entrance that hides the headline until a scroll completes is a defect if the person never scrolls.

## Forms, focus, and the path to the end

Submit every form with good data and with bad data. Empty required fields. A mistyped email. A too-long message. You are looking for a human sentence, a visible error, and a way to fix it without starting over. A red border with no words fails. A success state that does not say what happens next fails.

Tab through the page. You should be able to see where focus is, reach the button, and send the form without a mouse. The WCAG overview groups the guidelines under perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. QA does not need to become a legal audit to honor those four. It needs to catch a dialog you cannot escape, a label that is only a placeholder, and an error that appears far from the field.

Check the action on a phone with your thumb. The primary button should be reachable and distinct. If the only way to continue is a text link styled like a caption, fix the hierarchy. This is design QA. Engineering can help. The judgment is whether a person can finish.

Buy the thing, or book the thing, on a staging server if production would charge a customer. Go as far as the path allows. A checkout you have never completed is a rumor. Baymard Institute's average of documented cart-abandonment studies sits at 70.22 percent, and a long or fragile checkout is one of the reasons shoppers name. You will not fix every cause in a QA pass. You can refuse to launch a broken one.

Read the email that the form sends. The plain text version, not only the designed one. The subject line should say what happened. The reply-to should be a person. A form that succeeds on screen and vanishes into an unattended inbox is a failed path.

## Content that rots on launch day

Click every link in the navigation and the footer. Then click the links inside the body. A leftover staging URL, a partner you no longer work with, and a social profile for a renamed account are all launch blockers. They take minutes to fix and years to explain.

Look at images. The right crop. Alt text that describes the picture when the picture carries meaning. No giant file that exists only because the export was lazy. Hero images are part of loading performance. A beautiful photograph that blows the first paint is a design problem, not only an engineering one.

Read the legal lines you actually need: privacy, returns, the thing you promised in the hero. If the hero says free delivery over a threshold, the product page and the cart should say the same threshold. Contradictions are QA defects. They are also how support tickets start.

Check a logged-out window and a logged-in one if the product has accounts. The marketing site and the product should feel like the same company. Got Next, Leadly, and Trade Moai are public reminders that a product interface has a hierarchy of its own. QA includes the door between the site and the product, not only the campaign hero.

Spell the name of the company the same way everywhere. It sounds small. It is the kind of miss a careful customer sees first.

## Who does the pass, and what "fixed" means

The person who designed the page should do a pass, because they know which compromises were intentional. A second person should do a pass, because the designer will not see their own assumptions. The founder should do one path, the path they will brag about, on their own phone. If the founder cannot finish it, the launch is early.

Write findings as decisions, not as moods. "The error on the email field has no text." "The title on the pricing page is still the homepage title." "The layout shifts when the photograph loads." Assign an owner. A channel full of screenshots is not a list.

Separate blockers from later. A blocker stops the launch. A later item goes to the phase list you already agreed. QA is not a door for new pages. If a finding is really a new idea, mark it as a swap or a later phase. The scope you wrote is still the scope.

Define fixed as "checked again on the real page." A ticket moved to done without a second look is how the error text stays missing. On a Hanabi project the notes live with the other docs, and after delivery the client portal holds the updates so the launch list is not trapped in a chat.

## The hour before you share the URL

Do the path one last time on the production domain. Staging can lie about caching, images, and the title tag. Confirm the domain, the certificate, and the page you get when you are not logged in as an editor.

Confirm analytics receives the one action you care about, if measurement was in scope. Confirm you can edit a sentence without a developer, if that was the deal. Confirm the repository and the accounts are in the client's name.

Then stop. A launch does not need a new illustration discovered at 6 p.m. It needs the pages you scoped, in the states you listed, readable on a phone.

What you hand the next person, if there is a next person, should match what you just checked. The piece on [what to hand a developer with a design](/blog/what-to-hand-a-developer-with-a-design) is the next read if this QA pass found that the engineer had to invent the empty states. That invention should have arrived in the handoff, not in the last week.

When you want to see the standard applied to finished work, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The pages there had to survive the same kind of pass: real type, real states, and a job a stranger can finish.
